BERT4Rec explicitly acknowledges a mismatch between random masked reconstruction and next-item prediction; inference appends a mask and scores its hidden state. A 2024 encoder-only study, [Sequential Masked Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11150), reports gains from sliding windows and penultimate-token masking, supporting investigation of masking strategy rather than assuming stronger negative margins solve task alignment. Experiment hypothesis: retain one bidirectional BERT4Rec network, train on truncated prefixes ending in a reserved mask with the target absent, and compare terminal-only versus mixed terminal/reconstruction losses. This is an adaptation, not an established result on the pinned benchmark. [BERT4Rec paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06690).

Hardness and negative validity are separate concerns. [NARec (2025)](https://ietresearch.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1049/aie2.70004) reports benefits from batch/global negative selection and augmentation; [UFNRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04116) warns that sampled negatives can represent genuine interests, although its teacher mechanism should not be imported into this single-model experiment. A compatible hypothesis is moderate hard-negative sampling within the same network, excluding known training positives and duplicate target IDs; semantic filtering remains uncertain without relevance labels. Neither paper establishes that larger random-negative margins improve this benchmark’s HR@10.

Allocation snapshots cannot be verified from the supplied text: no counters or branch probabilities are provided. For mutually exclusive Bernoulli allocation, log eligible draws N, configured p, and actual branch counts; require n_A+n_B=N, with expected n_A=Np and standard deviation √[Np(1−p)] for independent fixed-p draws. Exactly equal counts are possible at p=0.5, but do not demonstrate Bernoulli sampling. Distinguish allocation counts from accepted negatives and loss weights before interpreting objective comparisons.
